name: CH334R
title: CH334/CH335: four-port USB 2.0 high-speed hub controller with multi-TT, CH334R in QSOP16
summary: A four-port USB 2.0 hub controller family. The upstream port runs at high or full speed, the four downstream ports at high, full or low speed, and each downstream port has its own transaction translator (MTT), so slower devices on different ports are served at the same time. An internal LDO makes the 3.3 V core supply from USB 5 V, the USB pull-ups and pull-downs and the crystal load capacitors are inside, and an internal clock allows crystal-free use. The models differ by package and by which extras they bring out: port power switching, over-current sensing, status LEDs, pin straps, an EEPROM port and, on CH335F, upstream port swapping. CH334R, in QSOP16, is the bare hub with none of these extras.

notes: CH335P and CH334P are the small-footprint choices; CH335F brings out every function.
CH334S, CH334X, CH334Q and CH334L are not recommended for new designs, and CH334L is supplied only by lot booking.
CH334X replaces CH334Q: it adds per-port (dual independent) mode, drops GANG mode, has active-high PWREN outputs and runs from a 24 MHz crystal.

rows: Must equal VID_H+VID_L+PID_L+PID_H+1; if it does not, the whole EEPROM is ignored.
Bits 7-5 and bit 0 reserved. Bits 4, 3, 2, 1: a 1 marks the device on downstream port 4, 3, 2, 1 as not removable.
Maximum operating current, in units of 2mA.
Validity mark for CFG at 0Ah; CFG counts only when this byte is 5Ah.

Bit7: reserved. Bit6: EEPROM write permission, 0 = write protected, 1 = may be rewritten by the USB tool. Bit5: OC_LEVEL, over-current threshold: 0 (default) = 2.4V with weak pull-up, 1 = 4.1V with weak pull-down; 4.1V is for the simplified PMOS power control, 2.4V otherwise. Bit4: reserved, must be 1. Bit3: reserved, must be 0. Bit2: SELF_POWER, 1 (default, recommended) = self-powered, 0 = bus-powered; 0 acts as PSELF held low. Bit1: INDICATOR_EN, LED indicator enable, default 0, 1 = enabled. Bit0: GANG_MODE, 1 (default) = all-port over-current detection, 0 = per-port detection; 0 acts as a pull-down on PGANG or LED2.
notes: 57h has bit 1 set, while bit 1 (INDICATOR_EN) is given a default of 0.

circuits.title: Per-port power switching and per-port over-current sensing (Figure 3-1-1)
circuits.description: Each downstream port has its own current-limited switch, enabled by its own PWRENn# line, with the switch's open-drain fault flag returned to the matching OVCURn# input. VBUS1 to VBUS4 go to the VBUS pins of downstream ports 1 to 4. C4 holds up the shared 5 V input; C11 to C14 are the per-port bulk capacitors.
notes: R11 to R14 can be left off with OC_LEVEL = 0, since OVCURn# then has a weak internal pull-up.
This mode needs GANG_MODE = 0 (per-port detection).

circuits.title: One shared switch with fused ports and per-port sensing (Figure 3-1-2)
circuits.description: A single switch U5, driven by PWREN#, feeds a common VBUS-ALL rail; each port then takes its VBUS through a 500 mA fusible resistor. A 12K/15K divider from each port's VBUS feeds its OVCURn# input. This is the non-preferred way of doing whole-control, per-port sensing.
notes: Without power control, U5 and C4 are left out and VBUS-ALL is joined to 5V.
U5's FLAG output is not connected.

circuits.title: GANG mode: one switch, one fault flag (Figure 3-1-3)
circuits.description: One current-limited switch, enabled by PWREN#, powers all four downstream VBUS pins from one rail; its fault flag goes to OVCUR#.
notes: R11 can be left off in the default configuration; C11 is sized to suit.

circuits.title: Simplified GANG power control with a PMOS switch (Figure 3-1-4)
circuits.description: PWREN# connects to the PMOS gate through the green LED D10, with R10 from the gate to 5 V. A 1 A fuse follows the switch onto VBUS-ALL. R11 and R15 divide VBUS-ALL into OVCUR#, so that with OC_LEVEL = 0 an over-current is flagged when VBUS falls to about 4 V.
notes: A principle sketch only.
With OC_LEVEL = 1, R15 is removed and R11 becomes 1K.

circuits.title: Reset from an MCU pin without enabling CDP (Figure 3-2-2)
circuits.description: A Schottky diode in series, cathode toward the MCU, lets the MCU pull RESET#/CDP low but never drive it high, so a high MCU pin during power-up cannot enable CDP charging or block low-power sleep.

circuits.title: One status LED on LED4 (Figure 3-3-1)
circuits.description: An LED from VDD33 into LED4 through R9: on while the hub is active, off while it is suspended.
notes: R9 can be 200Ω to 1KΩ.

circuits.title: Five LEDs on CH335 with the PGANG strap (Figure 3-3-2)
circuits.description: Four green port LEDs sit in back-to-back pairs between LED1 or LED2 (each through 220 Ω) and LED4; the ACTIVE LED hangs from VDD33 on LED4 through R9. To strap PGANG low, R4 (3.9 kΩ) runs from LED2 to LED3, which is held low during reset; D5 keeps R4 from pulling LED3 down when LED3 is the port-swap input.

parts.note: fitted only to strap PGANG low
fitted only with R4 when LED3 controls port swapping

notes: Keeping the default GANG mode: R4 and D5 are removed.
Port swap not enabled: D5 can be replaced by a short.

circuits.title: Timed pull-down for the PGANG strap (Figure 3-3-2A)
circuits.description: Replaces R4 and D5 of the CH335 five-LED circuit. The falling edge on LED3 at power-up or reset is coupled through C41 and briefly turns on Q41, which charges the gate node of Q42 (C42 is discharged); Q42 then pulls LED2/PGANG low through R4 while R42 bleeds the node down. Once that time has passed the pull-down lets go, so LED3 being low later in suspend cannot faintly light the PORT3 LED.

circuits.title: Five LEDs on CH334U and CH334F (Figure 3-3-3)
circuits.description: The same back-to-back pairs as on CH335, with no strap parts, since CH334U and CH334F have their own PSELF pin and no per-port sensing. A green LED lit means its port is working; off means nothing attached or the port is suspended. Which LED goes with which port can be customised, and every LED is optional.

circuits.title: Nine LEDs on CH335 (Figure 3-3-4)
circuits.description: The five-LED scheme plus four red LEDs: LED1 and LED2 each drive a red pair toward LED3 and a green pair toward LED4, every pair through its own 220 Ω resistor. A red LED on a port signals a fault such as over-current or transfer errors.
notes: Needs a CH335 with upstream port swapping off, or LED3 being pulled low would swap the ports.

circuits.title: LED on PGANG, default strap (Figure 3-3-5, left)
circuits.description: With PGANG left to its internal pull-up (all-port mode), PGANG drives low when active, lighting the LED from VDD33 through R9; the LED is off in suspend.

circuits.title: LED on PGANG with the pull-down strap (Figure 3-3-5, right)
circuits.description: R4 straps PGANG low (per-port sensing); the output sense is then inverted, so PGANG drives high when active and lights the LED to ground through R9; off in suspend.

circuits.title: PGANG switching power to other devices (Figure 3-3-6)
circuits.description: PGANG's static output pulls the PMOS gate low through the green LED, switching 5 V onto VAUX for other devices; when PGANG goes high in suspend the PMOS turns off and those devices lose power.

circuits.title: External configuration EEPROM (Figure 3-4)
circuits.description: A 24C02 at address 0, write protect and address pins grounded, shares LED3 (as SCL) and LED4 (as SDA). No pull-up resistors are fitted; the SDA pin has its own pull-up current. The LEDs on those pins can stay.

circuits.title: Schottky isolation of VBUS and an external supply (Figure 3-6-1)
circuits.description: Schottky diodes D1 (from the upstream VIN) and D2 (from the external input P6) both feed the 5V rail, so neither supply can back-feed the other; the downstream VBUS then sits at about 4.7 V or lower. The 5V rail feeds V5 through R1 and the downstream VBUS through switch U5. R31 (2.2 kΩ) from VEXT and R32 (4.7 kΩ) to ground form an optional divider on PSELF that selects bus or self power automatically.

parts.note: USB current-limited power switch, drawn as a switch and fuse between VIN and VOUT

circuits.title: Ideal-diode isolation of VBUS and an external supply (Figure 3-6-2)
circuits.description: The CH213 ideal diode U3 passes the upstream VIN onto the 5V rail and blocks the external supply on P6 from back-feeding the upstream VBUS. At 500 mA its drop is about a third of a Schottky's, leaving about 4.9 V at the downstream VBUS. The chip's V5 is fed from VIN through R1, ahead of U3, so U3 also gives the upstream VBUS simple over-current and short-circuit protection without a CH217.

parts.note: USB current-limited power switch, drawn as a switch and fuse between VIN and VOUT

circuits.title: Simplified bus-powered hub with CH334R (Section 6.1)
circuits.description: The minimal hub. Upstream 5 V from P0 feeds V5 through R0, and the internal LDO makes VDD33. The 12 MHz crystal goes straight across XI and XO with no load capacitors, since about 16 pF is built in. The four downstream ports share one VBUS rail taken from the upstream 5 V through a 1 A fuse, with 220 µF bulk on it. RESET#/CDP is left open.

parts.note: 100mA fuse resistor; 0Ω in the simplest build
fuse resistor; a USB current-limited switch can replace it

notes: An over-voltage protector, if used, goes on V5.
For industrial use V5 and VDD33 can both run from an outside 3.3 V supply instead of the LDO.

circuits.title: Crystal-free bus-powered hub with CH335P (Section 6.2)
circuits.description: No crystal: XI is grounded and XO left open, selecting the internal clock. The downstream VBUS rail is fed from the upstream 5 V through a CH213 ideal diode, whose own current limit and short-circuit protection replace the fuse of the basic circuit.

parts.note: low-drop ideal diode with current limit

notes: Crystal-free running is a configurable option, not on by default in every package; some figures may fall outside the USB specification, so it suits only applications that are not timing-critical.

circuits.title: CH334R hub with an external power input (Section 6.3)
circuits.description: As the basic bus-powered hub, with a second 5 V input P6 on the downstream VBUS rail (the 5V and VBUS labels are one net). The CH213 ideal diode from the upstream 5 V keeps P6's supply from flowing back into the host when the host is off, and its current limit replaces the fuse. The chip itself stays powered from the upstream port through R1.

parts.note: low-drop ideal diode with current limit

notes: The supply on P6 needs its own over-current and short-circuit protection; failing that, fit a fuse resistor from P6 to 5V, or a USB power switch from 5V to VBUS.

circuits.title: CH335F hub with per-port switching and sensing (Section 6.5)
circuits.description: A full hub for a computer or a stand-alone hub box. Each downstream port has its own CH217A switch, enabled by its PWRENn# line, with R21 to R24 setting its current limit to suit the supply; each switch's FLAG# reports over-current or over-temperature on the matching OVCURn#, which has its own pull-up by default. External 5 V on P6 feeds the switches, and the CH213 ideal diode keeps it out of the upstream port. A 24C02 on LED3/LED4 holds the configuration alongside five status LEDs; R4 and D5 strap PGANG low for per-port sensing. An MCU can swap the upstream port with port 1 by driving LED3 through R3.

parts.note: low-drop ideal diode with current limit

notes: R3 can be 470Ω to 1.5KΩ.
On a CH335 with port swapping off, D5 is shorted and D5 and R3 removed.
Without P6, or when backflow does not matter, U3 is left out and VIN joined to +5.
Recommended additions: over-voltage protection on VIN and ESD protection on every USB line, for example CH412K with its VCC on 3V3.

circuits.title: CH334F hub with GANG switching and sensing (Section 6.6)
circuits.description: One CH217A switch, enabled by PWREN#, powers all four downstream VBUS pins from the upstream 5 V, with R21 setting its current limit; its FLAG# goes to OVCUR#. The chip runs from the same 5 V through R1 into V5. A 24C02 on LED3/LED4 holds the configuration, and five LEDs show port status. PSELF is left open, so the default self-powered setting applies.

operation.text: Inside are an upstream transceiver, four downstream transceivers, a high-speed and a full/low-speed repeater, four transaction translators (TTs), routing logic, a hub controller with RAM and ROM, an LED controller and an I2C port. The controller behaves like a small MCU managing everything. When a downstream device runs at the upstream port's speed, the routing logic joins it to the repeater; at a different speed it is joined to a TT.

In single-TT (STT) operation one translator is time-shared among all four downstream ports. In multi-TT (MTT) operation each port has its own translator working in parallel, so ports moving a lot of data at once each get fuller bandwidth, four times the total of STT. Every model in the family runs MTT.
The upstream port runs USB 2.0 high speed or full speed; each downstream port runs high speed (480 Mbps), full speed (12 Mbps) or low speed (1.5 Mbps). The hub is backward compatible with USB 1.1.

The upstream port has its 1.5 kΩ pull-up inside, and each downstream port has the host-side pull-downs inside. An LDO turns the USB bus voltage into the 3.3 V the chip runs on. A PLL multiplies the 12 MHz crystal or input up to 480 MHz for the PHYs, and an internal clock allows crystal-free builds. The USB pins withstand 6 kV ESD (HBM, Class 3A). Low-power LPM technology cuts consumption against earlier hub chips.

Three schemes exist: separate power switching and separate sensing for every port (dual independent); one power switch for all ports with separate sensing per port (whole control, solo inspection); and one switch with one sense line for all ports (GANG overall, the default). OVCUR inputs tolerate 5 V.

U5 to U8 in the per-port circuit are USB current-limited distribution switches with their own over-current detection, such as CH217. Where the hub has no separate 5 V supply, set their current limit with the ISET resistor to under 1 A, or even to 500 mA. Their FLAG outputs are open drain; with the default OC_LEVEL = 0, each OVCUR pin supplies a weak pull-up so no resistor is needed. The USB specification asks for at least 120 µF per port VBUS. Per-port mode needs GANG_MODE = 0.

The preferred way is the per-port circuit with PWREN# driving all four switches together. Because the four port capacitors then charge at the same moment, C4 should be at least their combined capacitance.

OC_LEVEL selects the OVCUR threshold: 0 (default) gives 2.4 V with a weak pull-up, 1 gives 4.1 V with a weak pull-down. The 4.1 V setting is for the simplified PMOS power control; otherwise 2.4 V is used.

An internal power-on reset holds the chip in reset for Trpor, about 5 to 14 ms, after power comes up, so an external reset is normally not needed. Chips whose lot number has 6 as its second-to-last digit wait about 12 ms; those with 1 there, the default supply, wait about 5 to 7 ms. If the supply drops below Vlvr in operation, the low-voltage reset holds the chip until the supply recovers and the same delay has run.
RESET#/CDP has an internal pull-up of about 25 kΩ. To reset the chip, drive the pin low through no more than 800 Ω for longer than 4 µs.

For a few milliseconds at power-up RESET#/CDP is read as a three-level input: both an internal pull-up and pull-down of about 25 kΩ are on, so an undriven pin sits near half of VDD33. Driven high then, CDP charging is enabled and low-power sleep is disabled; left floating, CDP stays off and sleep is allowed; driven low, the chip is reset. After power-up the pin returns to a plain pull-up. If an MCU pin drives RESET#/CDP and might be high at power-up, put a Schottky diode in series (cathode at the MCU) to keep CDP off and sleep current low. Type-C and USB PD fast charging can be added with a chip such as CH227.

Following USB 2.0, a port's green LED is on when the port is working and off when nothing is attached or it is suspended; its red LED is on when the port has a fault. CH334 and CH335 drive one-LED and five-LED schemes, and CH335 also nine LEDs. LED1 to LED4 are driven dynamically, time-shared. The port LED resistors (R5 to R8) can be 100 Ω to 1 kΩ. In the one-LED scheme the LED on LED4 is on while active and off in suspend, with R9 between 200 Ω and 1 kΩ.

On CH335, LED1/PSELF and LED2/PGANG can be pulled down during reset to set bus power or per-port sensing. They also drive LEDs, so they must not be tied straight to ground: fit 3.9 kΩ (3 to 5.1 kΩ) from LED1 or LED2 to LED3, which is driven low during reset. Where LED1 or LED2 already drives an LED, use EEPROM or factory configuration instead. A diode in series with that resistor stops it pulling LED3 low when LED3 is the port-swap input; without port swapping the diode can be a short.

LED3 on CH335 can also be an input that swaps the upstream port with downstream port 1, a configurable function chosen when ordering. It is enabled on chips whose lot number has 1 among its last six digits and ends in an even digit; these support only the five-LED scheme. Connect LED3 to an MCU GPIO through 1 kΩ: high (default) means no swap, low swaps the ports, and the chip may reset itself first depending on its state. On other lots swapping is off and LED3 serves the nine-LED scheme. If the strap resistor R4 is fitted and the MCU holds LED3 low to swap, the PORT3 LED may glow faintly in suspend when LED4 is pulled up; the timed pull-down circuit cures this. CH338 offers port swapping and SMBus-controlled isolation or extension instead.

PSELF is an input only, with a pull-up. PGANG is bidirectional with a pull-up: during reset it is read as the over-current mode strap, and afterwards it outputs the suspend or active state. Unlike LED4, PGANG drives statically, so an LED on it can use a larger resistor, and it can switch power to other devices so they turn off in suspend.

A two-wire I2C link reads an external EEPROM at address 0 for vendor ID, product ID and configuration. SCL runs at 187.5 kHz; SDA carries an internal pull-up of about 250 µA, so no external pull-ups are needed. The EEPROM shares LED3 and LED4 with the LEDs without conflict, in nine-, five-, one- or no-LED builds. Instead of an EEPROM, the built-in information memory can be customised in volume, for example to set the number of downstream ports or mark port devices as non-removable.
At power-up the chip loads its internal information memory first and then the external EEPROM. When the EEPROM checksum is wrong, all its data is discarded; when right, all of it is used.

Bus power comes from the upstream port (500 mA, 900 mA, 1.5 A and other standards); cable resistance and the hub's own current lower what reaches the downstream ports. Self power comes from an outside supply. The two voltages are never quite equal, so the hub must stop heavy current flowing between them, and must stop the outside supply feeding back into the host when the upstream port is off. Two Schottky diodes isolate both ways but leave the downstream VBUS at about 4.7 V or lower; a resistor divider (2.2 kΩ and 4.7 kΩ) from the outside supply to PSELF can select the mode automatically. An ideal diode such as CH213 in the upstream path drops about a third of a Schottky's voltage at 500 mA, leaving about 4.9 V at the downstream VBUS, and can also give the upstream VBUS simple over-current and short-circuit protection.
XI and XO carry about 16 pF of built-in oscillator capacitance; no external load capacitors should be added to the crystal. CH334X uses a 24 MHz crystal, every other model 12 MHz.

R0 in the V5 path is a 100 mA fuse resistor, or 0 Ω in the simplest build; an over-voltage protector, if fitted, goes on V5. Swapping the 5V-to-VBUS fuse for a USB current-limited switch gives quicker, better protection. CH334X and CH334Q have no LDO and no V5 pin; all their VDD33 pins take an outside 3.3 V.

For industrial use, both V5 and VDD33 can be fed from an outside 3.3 V supply. The chip then dissipates 85 mA × 3.3 V rather than 85 mA × 5 V, with less drop and less temperature rise; built this way it was measured working from -40 to 105 ℃, and briefly at 125 ℃ with some parameters out of limits. Fuse resistors and USB power switches may not be rated for such temperatures.

Plugging a device into a powered downstream port can make VBUS and 5V dip, trip the low-voltage reset and drop the whole hub off the bus. Remedies: a larger electrolytic on the 5 V rail (C4) within what the USB specification allows; more capacitance on the LDO output (C8, for example 22 µF); feeding V5 and VDD33 from an outside 3.3 V with more capacitance on it; or a stronger 5 V supply or self power, and a better USB cable.

The internal clock lets the 12 MHz crystal (24 MHz on CH334X) be removed, saving size, cost and EMI; some figures may then drift outside the USB specification, so it suits applications that are not timing-critical. It is a configurable option, off by default on CH335 and some CH334 packages, chosen when ordering. Leave XO open and ground XI to select it; otherwise fit the crystal.

With an outside supply on P6, an ideal diode such as CH213 between the upstream 5 V and the downstream rail keeps the outside supply from reaching the upstream VBUS, for instance when the host computer is off. A Schottky diode can stand in if its drop is low enough: at 300 mA a Schottky drops about 0.3 V and the ideal diode about 0.05 V. Backflow from the upstream port into P6 is normally ignored, since P6 carries no load.

With a 3.3 V supply on the board, connect V5 and VDD33 both to it; C8 and C2 may then be merged into one 1 µF capacitor. Where downstream devices are fixed on the board, they can be marked non-removable, fed straight from 5 V, and over-current detection simplified or dropped.
Size the VIN, +5V, VOUT (VBUS) and P6 tracks and every port's ground path for the real current, as wide as possible, with several vias in parallel at each layer change.
